To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have shown that coeliac disease is associated with persistent changes in innate immune cell subsets in both blood and small intestine.
coeliac disease patients have persistent changes in circulating and intestinal γδ T cell subsets, invariant natural killer T cells, and mucosa associated invariant T cells.

coeliac disease patients, both adults and children, have a persistent aberrant innate lymphoid profile, which is characterised by a skewing of the γδ T cell compartment toward Vδ1 cells, and a loss of CD56+ T and NK cells, in both blood and gut, even after gluten-free diet.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the role of the innate lymphocyte populations in the pathogenesis of coeliac disease.
the role of innate lymphocytes in the pathogenesis and progression of coeliac disease.
the role of γδ T cell subsets in coeliac disease and other inflammatory conditions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
coeliac disease is a complex disease that affects the innate immune system as well as the adaptive immune system.
the innate immune system is involved in the pathogenesis of coeliac disease, and that the Vδ1 subset may play an important role.
coeliac disease is an autoimmune disease that affects the gut, with the immune response being triggered by the ingestion of gluten.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we show a persistent aberrant innate lymphoid profile in coeliac patients, persisting even in the absence of dietary gluten, which could lead to impaired immunity and potentially account for the high incidence of autoimmune comorbidities.
we have shown that there is a profound skewing of the γδ T cell compartment in coeliac disease.

we have identified a persistent abnormality of innate immune cell numbers in the blood of coeliac disease patients and a profound change in the γδ T cell subset profile in the small intestinal mucosa of both children and adults with coeliac disease.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the innate immune system plays a key role in the pathogenesis of coeliac disease.
the innate immune system is profoundly affected in coeliac disease.
there is an aberrant innate lymphocytic response in coeliac patients.
